question: A 12-year-old boy presents with 24 hours of central abdominal pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, with a temperature of 38.2°C and localised tenderness. Alvarado score is 8. Which imaging investigation is most appropriate as the first step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is the most sensitive and specific modality for appendicitis but involves ionising radiation — a significant concern in a child. In children and young, thin adults, ultrasound should always be attempted first. CT is reserved for inconclusive USG or when complications such as perforation and abscess need delineation.

Correct. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging in children, young adults, and pregnant women because it uses no radiation. A positive ultrasound (non-compressible appendix ≥6 mm, periappendiceal echogenic fat, hyperaemia on Doppler) is highly specific. If ultrasound is inconclusive, CT or MRI (in pregnancy) follows.

Plain X-ray is insensitive and non-specific for appendicitis. An appendicolith (faecolith) may rarely be visible, but plain X-ray has no diagnostic role in suspected appendicitis. It has been largely abandoned in favour of ultrasound and CT.

MRI has high sensitivity for appendicitis without radiation and is the preferred alternative to CT in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive. However, it is slower and less available than USG or CT, and in children ultrasound is the standard first-line investigation.

overallFeedback.feedback: In children and pregnant women, ultrasound is the first-line imaging for suspected appendicitis because it avoids radiation. CT is reserved for inconclusive USG or when complications are suspected.
Correct. Ultrasound first in children — no radiation, widely available, and adequately sensitive when the appendix is visualised.
